messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rodrigo is a 35-year-old Latin American musician, married, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 44 following a life-threatening accident that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. He was driving home late after a recording session when a driver ran a red light and struck his vehicle at high speed on the passenger side. Rodrigo was conscious throughout, trapped in the wreckage for nearly forty minutes, aware of the smell of fuel and the sound of metal settling around him. The other driver was cited but faced no meaningful legal consequence, a fact that has never left Rodrigo's mind. When he was finally extracted and taken to hospital, he was told he had come within inches of a more catastrophic injury. He was discharged within days, and for a time he told himself he was fine.

The months that followed told a different story. Rodrigo found that when he sat down and deliberately tried to reconstruct what had happened — to make sense of it, to place it in order — he could not. The memory refused to cohere. What came instead were fragments: the white glare of headlights, a sensation of weightlessness, the voice of a paramedic whose face he cannot picture. These pieces arrived without sequence or context, and the gaps between them felt enormous. He had the persistent, unsettling sense that he was only remembering parts of what happened and that the rest had been taken from him. This fractured quality of the memory fed directly into his interpretation of events: if he could not hold the full picture, then perhaps what had been done to him was even worse than he could consciously access. The incompleteness of the memory deepened his conviction that something profoundly unjust had occurred and that no one had been held accountable for it.

These appraisals — that his life had been destroyed, that a terrible wrong had gone unanswered — became the lens through which he viewed almost everything. He had come to believe that the rage he felt toward the other driver was not a normal response to injustice but evidence of something dangerous inside him, a force he was certain he could not control if it were ever fully released. This fear of his own anger became a reason, in his mind, to keep the accident sealed away. Thinking about the event, or allowing others to draw him into conversation about it, felt like opening a door he could not close again. So he stopped. He deflected questions from his wife with brief reassurances. He declined to discuss the accident with anyone. And he began filling every available hour with other people — bandmates, friends, extended family — so that he was never alone long enough for his own thoughts to find him. The constant socialising was not pleasure; it was management.

The irony was that keeping the memory at arm's length through avoidance and relentless company only ensured it stayed broken. Because Rodrigo never sat with the fragments long enough to work through them, they remained disconnected and unprocessed, and the gaps in the memory continued to feel threatening rather than simply incomplete. The fragmented, inaccessible quality of what he did remember, in turn, renewed his sense that his life had been altered in ways he could not fully see or name — that something irreplaceable had been taken from him and never returned. In his work as a musician, where solitude and introspection had once been essential to his creative process, he now found he could not be alone in a studio without the anxiety rising. Sessions that used to last hours were cut short. Collaborations he once welcomed now served mainly as cover. His wife had noticed the change and had said so, more than once, and the distance between them had grown in ways neither had named directly.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a moment at a family gathering when a relative, meaning no harm, asked him casually how he was doing after the accident. He felt the anger rise so fast and so completely that he left the room without speaking. Standing outside, he was shaken — not by what he had done, but by how close it had felt. He came to the first session hoping, above all, that he was not the person he was afraid he had become.
